opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a useful analogy up to a point, and then it breaks down in some pretty instructive ways.

The part that I think is genuinely right is that a lot of what both humans and language models end up knowing isn't explicitly taught. Kids aren't handed a grammar of English; they pick it up from exposure. And similarly, nobody sits down and tells a language model what a noun phrase is or how coreference works, yet if you probe these models you find representations that look a lot like the abstractions linguists have been positing for decades. So there's something to the idea that rich structure can be induced from relatively unstructured experience, and that's an interesting result for cognitive science, not just for machine learning.

But the differences are at least as important. The most obvious one is scale. A child hears something on the order of tens of millions of words in their first several years, and these models are trained on trillions. That's a gap of many orders of magnitude, and it should make us cautious about drawing conclusions like "you don't need innate structure to learn language," because the models are getting a kind of input that no human ever gets.

The second difference is that human language learning is grounded and interactive. Children aren't passively reading text off the internet. They're learning language in the middle of trying to get things done: getting someone to hand them a cup, pointing at a dog, being corrected, being ignored. Language is tied to perception, to action, and to other minds with goals. Pretraining, at least in its classic form, strips almost all of that away. You just get the text, which is kind of the residue of all those communicative interactions, without the interactions themselves.

And I think one of the more interesting questions for the field is how much of that missing context can be recovered from text alone. My view is that more of it can be recovered than people initially expected, because text is produced by agents with beliefs and intentions, and to predict text well you end up having to model something about those agents. But "something" is doing a lot of work there. These models build models of communicative intent that are partial, sometimes incoherent, and not anchored to any particular perspective of their own.

So the way I'd summarize it is: pretraining isn't a good model of how humans learn language, but it's a really useful existence proof about what's learnable from a particular kind of data. And the places where the analogy fails, data efficiency, grounding, interaction, are probably exactly where we should look for what's still missing from current systems.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts children’s grounded, interactive learning with text-only pretraining and calls the analogy limited, but it does not clearly distinguish prediction’s broad usefulness for learning from whether pretraining matches the specific prediction problems humans face.

r002.rationale: It notes that models use far more data and cautions against concluding humans need no innate structure, but it does not ask what innate bias lets humans learn from much less data.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that an account of initial human learning biases must avoid presupposing that their origins already encountered the adult capabilities later acquired.

r004.rationale: The response does not argue that training models on adult-like capabilities reveals little about the origins of humans’ initial learning biases.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the analogy is useful in exactly one direction and misleading in the other.

The useful direction is that it reminds us how much structure you can get from prediction alone. Before the big pretraining results, a lot of people in my field, myself included, assumed that if you wanted a system to learn syntax, or something like compositional meaning, you had to build the inductive bias in. The empirical story of the last several years is that next-token prediction over enough text gets you surprisingly far on those fronts. That's at least consistent with the more usage-based accounts of human acquisition, where kids are tracking distributional statistics and generalizing from them. So pretraining is a nice existence proof that the statistical route is less hopeless than the old poverty-of-the-stimulus arguments suggested.

Where I think the analogy breaks down is almost everything else about the learning situation. A child hears something on the order of tens of millions of words by the time they're producing fluent speech. A frontier model sees trillions. That's not a rounding error, that's a different regime. The child's input is also interactive and grounded. They get to point at things, they get corrected, they get to test a hypothesis by saying something and seeing what happens. The model gets a static corpus that was written by people who already had all of this knowledge, so a lot of what looks like learning is really compression of other people's learning.

The other thing I'd push on is the word "learning" itself. When we say a model learned something in pretraining, we usually mean its parameters moved. When we say a kid learned something, we often mean they can now use it flexibly in a new context, and that they'll keep refining it. Models do some of that in context, and I actually find in-context learning the more interesting place to look for the analogy. But the pretraining phase itself looks less like childhood and more like something that has no real human analog. It's closer to the species-level accumulation of knowledge than to the individual's acquisition of it.

So my honest assessment is that it's a good analogy for motivating hypotheses and a bad one for drawing conclusions. If someone says "models learn syntax from statistics, therefore humans must too," that's not licensed. If someone says "here's something a model does without explicit supervision, let's go check whether kids show a similar signature," that's exactly the kind of work I'd like to see more of.

r001.rationale: The response says prediction alone can produce substantial linguistic structure, then explains why model pretraining differs from human learning in scale, interactivity, and grounding.

r002.rationale: It compares the amount of data children and models receive, but does not ask what innate inductive bias enables children to learn with less data.

r003.rationale: It notes that models train on text written by people who already have knowledge, but does not state that an explanation of humans’ initial learning biases must avoid presupposing exposure to adult capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says model pretraining is a poor basis for drawing conclusions about human learning, but does not argue that training on adult-like capabilities reveals little about the origins of humans’ initial learning biases.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is useful, but we have to be specific about what part of human learning we mean. Humans learn an enormous amount from language. I can tell you about a place you’ve never visited or explain how to do something you’ve never done, and that changes what you know and how you act. So the idea that learning from language can produce fairly general capabilities doesn’t seem surprising to me.

But language-model pretraining is also very different from the way a child learns. A child is interacting with the world, taking actions, seeing their consequences, and asking questions. Language comes into that process alongside perception and social interaction. A language model is typically learning from a fixed collection of text, without much control over what information it encounters.

So I’d distinguish two questions: how much can you learn from language alone, and is that how humans actually learn? These models give us a really interesting way to investigate the first question. Their success doesn’t, by itself, settle the second.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts learning from text with children’s interactive learning, but it does not discuss prediction or distinguish broad usefulness of prediction from resemblance to human prediction problems.

r002.rationale: It does not ask what innate inductive bias lets humans learn language from far less data.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether explaining initial learning biases may presuppose prior exposure to adult capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says model success does not settle how humans learn, but does not argue that training on adult-like capabilities reveals little about the origins of humans’ initial learning biases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful analogy in some respects, but we should be careful about what we’re comparing. Humans learn a tremendous amount from language. Most of what I know about the world isn’t something I’ve personally observed or experimented with; somebody told me about it, or I read it somewhere. So the idea that you can acquire fairly rich knowledge just by learning from linguistic input doesn’t strike me as surprising in itself.

But human learning also happens in a much broader context. We perceive things, take actions, and see what happens. And when we encounter language, we’re often trying to understand what another person wants us to know or do. Predicting the next word might encourage a model to learn some of the same underlying structure, but that doesn’t mean the learning process is the same.

So I’d separate two questions: can this training procedure produce abilities that resemble human abilities, and is it a good account of how humans acquire those abilities? I think the evidence for the first is much stronger than the evidence for the second. The interesting thing is to figure out where the similarities hold, where they break down, and what those differences tell us about the information each learner has access to.

r001.rationale: The response says linguistic prediction can support rich learning, while emphasizing that humans also learn through perception and action and that next-word prediction does not make the learning processes the same.

r002.rationale: It does not ask what innate bias enables humans to learn language from far less data than current models.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether an explanation of initial learning biases presupposes adult capabilities.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss whether training models on adult-like capabilities reveals the origins of humans’ initial learning biases.
